group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 52-year-old man who works as a city bus mechanic and lives with his spouse in a single-story ranch house walked into the emergency department near dawn after two days of progressive exertional shortness of breath, pleuritic right-sided chest tightness, and a dry cough that turned scantly productive overnight; he stated he swallowed no antipyretics, puffed no rescue inhaler, took no home diuretic dose, and avoided his portable oxygen concentrator on the ride in because “I want the numbers naked.” His background is notable for an anterior wall myocardial infarction seven years ago that left a chronically reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction around one-third by his last cardiology ultrasound, and for a small lacunar infarct in the left internal capsule two years ago that produced a transient right-hand clumsiness but resolved without functional limitation—he remains on low-dose aspirin and high-intensity statin for both conditions. He never required dialysis, has normal hepatic panels on previous annual bloodwork, has no record of malignancy, and has always lived independently, climbing the short flight of steps to his porch daily without home-health assistance. He quit smoking after a 25-pack-year exposure when the infarct occurred, drinks one bottle of beer with Saturday dinner, and denies illicit drug use. Immunization registry shows completion of both pneumococcal formulations and last autumn’s influenza vaccine. On arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences albeit pausing for breath every few words, alert to name, date, and surroundings and able to recall three objects at five minutes. Skin was warm, lightly diaphoretic, with capillary refill under two seconds; mucous membranes appeared tacky, and there was no peripheral edema. Untreated triage vitals on ambient air at this sea-level institution were: oral temperature 99.4 °F (37.4 °C), a rapid regular radial pulse of 148 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry as sinus tachycardia, non-invasive right-arm blood pressure 148/86 mm Hg verified manually, respirations 30 per minute with mild intercostal recruitment, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 88 % and 90 %. Neck veins tracked 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, similar to previous cardiology notes. Cardiac auscultation revealed a brisk S1/S2 with a soft third component long documented on office exams and no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination showed coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower posterior lung zone and scattered end-expiratory pops in the left base; percussion was resonant throughout, and both costophrenic angles were sharp. Abdomen was flat, nontender, with normal hepatic span by percussion; no pulsatile masses or organomegaly were felt. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated equal reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, normal speech cadence, and 5/5 symmetric strength without pronator drift. Capillary glucose measured at the bedside before vascular access was 128 mg/dL. Within ten minutes of bay entry two 20-gauge peripheral lines were placed and flushed with only 2 mL heparinized saline each; venous chemistries, complete blood count, and a right radial arterial sample were obtained before any medication, fluid, or oxygen was administered. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 150 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 112 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL—values moderately hypernatremic and mildly azotemic compared with prior clinic results. Hemogram showed leukocytes 14.2 × 10⁹/L with 85 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 37 %, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, and platelets 242 × 10⁹/L. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pH 7.47, PaCO₂ 32 mm Hg, PaO₂ 66 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, indicating a primary respiratory alkalosis with mild hypoxemia. Serum lactate was 1.8 mmol/L and high-sensitivity troponin matched baseline undetectable levels. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 148 bpm with unchanged left-bundle branch block morphology from old tracings but no new ischemic pattern. Portable postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs obtained fifteen minutes into the encounter—before antibiotics, bronchodilators, diuretics, or supplemental oxygen—demonstrated a patchy consolidation occupying the posterior segment of the right lower lobe with silhouetting of the right hemidiaphragm, preserved cardiac outline, and no blunting or layering opacity in either costophrenic recess. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory prior to any empiric therapy. Up to the moment this narrative is filed he remains on 21 % inspired oxygen, has received no intravenous fluids beyond the minimal flushes, no vasoactive agents, no anti-pyretics, and no bronchodilators, ensuring that every vital sign, laboratory value, and imaging finding recorded above reflects his untreated presentation state.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the adult Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) using untreated admission data.
- Demographics: a man's baseline is his age in years → 52. Lives at home, so no nursing-home points → 0.
- Comorbidities: chronic systolic heart failure → 10; prior lacunar stroke (cerebrovascular disease) → 10. No malignancy, chronic liver disease, or chronic renal disease documented → 0 each.
- Examination: respiratory rate 30/min meets ≥30 → 20; pulse 148/min meets ≥125 → 10. Mentation normal, systolic BP 148 (not <90 mm Hg), temperature 37.4°C (neither <35 nor ≥40) → 0 each.
- Laboratory criteria: pH 7.47 (not <7.35), BUN 28 (not ≥30 mg/dL), sodium 150 (not <130 mEq/L), glucose 128 (not ≥250 mg/dL), and hematocrit 37% (not <30%) → 0 each. Using the measured room-air arterial PaO₂ of 66 mm Hg, the <60 mm Hg oxygenation criterion is not met → 0; the pulse oximeter reading is not scored separately.
- Imaging: no pleural effusion → 0.
Sum: 52 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 102 (PSI class IV).
Final answer: 102
